speaker: Tom Mueller
title: Impulse Space CEO Tom Mueller - Propulsion, and Rocket Engines - NSF Live
question: In liquid rocket engine design, why does full-flow staged combustion make much more sense for a sea-level booster than for a vacuum upper-stage engine?
guest: It is not full flow, and there is a reason why I do not think it makes sense for our space engine to be full flow. It is oxygen-rich staged combustion, which seems like the perfect cycle for an engine like this. Full flow is for when you need to get as much chamber pressure as possible, which is a booster engine—especially a booster engine where you want to take as much payload to Mars as possible. That is why Raptor, the RD-180, or the Space Shuttle Main Engine have crazy high chamber pressures. Your performance is your pressure ratio from chamber pressure to exit pressure. At sea level, your exit pressure is 15 PSI, so you cannot get a high ratio without going high on chamber pressure. In the vacuum of space, you are dividing by zero—it is zero exit pressure, so you can put as much nozzle on the engine as you want. Then it just becomes how much will fit and what the diminishing returns are. Our engine originally had a 200 area ratio, and when we looked at packaging we cut it to 160 because we did not gain that much on the extra 40 and it fits better.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Full-flow staged combustion (FFSC) exists mainly to deliver very high chamber pressure, and chamber pressure matters far more at sea level than in vacuum.

A booster has to expand its exhaust against ambient pressure, so the nozzle's usable expansion ratio is capped by the exit pressure it can tolerate before flow separation. The only way to get a larger expansion ratio, and thus higher specific impulse, is to raise chamber pressure. High pressure also shrinks the engine for a given thrust, improving thrust-to-weight and thrust per unit of base area, which is critical when packing many engines under a booster and fighting gravity losses. FFSC maximizes available turbine power by sending all of both propellants through the turbines, reaching these pressures at cooler, gentler turbine temperatures, which also helps reusability.

In vacuum, expansion ratio is limited only by nozzle size and mass, not ambient pressure. Specific impulse depends only weakly on chamber pressure, and thrust-to-weight matters less. Simpler expander or gas-generator cycles therefore get nearly the same performance, so FFSC's two preburners, two turbopumps and added complexity and mass buy little.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer:
Full-flow staged combustion (FFSC) excels by enabling extreme chamber pressures: routing all propellant through dual preburners maximizes turbine mass flow, delivering massive pumping power at benign temperatures suited for reusable boosters. At sea level, ultra-high chamber pressure is essential because atmospheric pressure triggers nozzle flow separation if exhaust overexpands. Raising chamber pressure is therefore the primary way to achieve high expansion ratios, high sea-level specific impulse, and compact, high-thrust engines that cluster tightly onto a booster base.

In vacuum, zero ambient pressure eliminates flow separation, allowing moderate-pressure engines to reach large expansion ratios and near-maximum specific impulse simply by using a larger nozzle bell. Meanwhile, upper-stage dry mass directly penalizes payload capacity, and lower upper-stage thrust makes scaling down high-pressure turbomachinery difficult and inefficient. Because FFSC demands dual preburners, heavy high-pressure hardware, and complex hot-gas plumbing, simpler designs like the closed expander cycle achieve comparable vacuum efficiency with less mass and risk, leaving manufacturing commonality with a booster as the main reason to use FFSC on an upper stage.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Full-flow staged combustion (FFSC) is mainly a way to reach very high chamber pressure. All of both propellants pass through the turbines, so you get a lot of turbine power at relatively mild turbine temperatures, and no propellant is dumped overboard. That pressure helps a sea-level booster much more than a vacuum engine.

At sea level, the surrounding air limits how far the nozzle can expand the exhaust before the flow separates from the nozzle wall. Higher chamber pressure lets you use a larger expansion ratio and get more specific impulse (efficiency) without separation. It also packs more thrust into a smaller, lighter engine. That matters when you need huge liftoff thrust and have to fit many engines under a fixed base area.

In vacuum there is no air pushing back, so efficiency depends mostly on the nozzle's expansion ratio, and that is limited by nozzle size and mass, not chamber pressure. Upper stages also need modest thrust. Simpler cycles, like the RL10's expander cycle or a gas generator whose small propellant loss barely matters, reach nearly the same efficiency. They do it without FFSC's two preburners, oxygen-rich hot-gas hardware, cost and development risk.

SpaceX's Raptor Vacuum uses FFSC largely to share hardware with the booster's Raptor, not because the cycle is best for vacuum use.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer:
Full-flow staged combustion shines on a sea-level booster because its dual preburners route all of the propellant through the turbines, enabling extreme chamber pressures and high thrust-to-weight ratios without overheating turbine hardware. At sea level, atmospheric backpressure limits nozzle expansion, so achieving high specific impulse and compact, high-thrust packaging requires very high chamber pressure to overcome ambient pressure and minimize gravity losses at liftoff.

In a vacuum upper stage, those advantages largely disappear while the penalties become severe. Without ambient air resisting the exhaust, high specific impulse comes primarily from a large nozzle expansion ratio rather than extreme chamber pressure, so simpler cycles like expander or conventional staged combustion can nearly match full-flow efficiency. Meanwhile, upper stages are far more sensitive to dry mass—every extra kilogram of engine directly subtracts from payload—and full-flow's twin preburners, dual turbopumps, and heavy high-pressure plumbing add mass, complexity, and cost while complicating the deep throttling and multiple restarts upper stages often need.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
Full-flow staged combustion earns its complexity on a sea-level booster because it can support very high chamber pressure. Sending the full propellant flow through the turbines lets them drive powerful pumps at lower turbine temperatures. High chamber pressure gives the booster more thrust from a compact engine and lets it use a larger nozzle expansion ratio before atmospheric backpressure causes flow separation.

In vacuum, backpressure disappears. An upper-stage engine can use a large expansion ratio even at modest chamber pressure, and at a fixed expansion ratio, raising chamber pressure has little direct effect on ideal vacuum specific impulse. The full-flow cycle’s extra hardware and complexity are therefore harder to justify on a stage where dry mass matters especially. It can still make sense if the upper stage needs high thrust in a tight envelope or can share an engine design with the booster.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
Full-flow staged combustion is most attractive when very high chamber pressure is worth the complexity. A sea-level booster needs high thrust from a limited base area. For a given thrust, higher chamber pressure allows a smaller nozzle throat. It also lets the nozzle expand the exhaust farther before its exit pressure falls to ambient pressure. Full-flow staged combustion can supply the pump power needed for that pressure while keeping turbine temperatures relatively low, an advantage for a reusable booster.

In vacuum, an upper stage can use a large nozzle expansion ratio even at moderate chamber pressure because there is no atmospheric back pressure. Full flow still offers benefits, but the extra plumbing and machinery have to earn their place through better performance or lower overall engine mass. Every kilogram of engine mass reaches orbit with the stage, so a simpler cycle can deliver more payload.
